source.title: Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance
source.authors: Jiasheng Ye; Peiju Liu; Tianxiang Sun; Yunhua Zhou; Jun Zhan; Xi-Peng Qiu

record.tranche_reason: The study fits power laws to language-model validation loss as training steps and model size vary, then tests predictions on larger runs.
record.gate_note: The study's data-mixing-law results and data-mixture optimization comparisons are not rows: they measure mixture effects, not the scaling-law claims. Statements citing other studies' scaling results are also excluded.
record.test_reason: The paper's main subject is a data-mixing law, but Appendices D.2 and F.3 directly check power-law fits of loss against training steps and model size by extrapolating them to larger runs. Those results bear on V1 and V2. The Figure 22 nested forecasts bear on V2 only weakly, because the pipeline also includes the mixing law. The scaling laws are mainly a tool here, so this is a weak T1, close to T4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is incomplete. The authors mainly conclude that loss is quantitatively predictable from the data-mixture proportions (data mixing laws). They also conclude that nesting step and model-size scaling laws with the mixing law lets small-scale runs optimise the mixture for a 1B, 100B-token model, matching the default mixture trained for 48% more steps. They note errors accumulate across the nested steps and that the Fig. 22 predictions underestimate the actual losses.
record.recipe_differences: Uses validation loss and power-law scaling in model size and training amount, but fits step and model-size laws sequentially rather than fitting a joint law; experiments use Pythia architectures and a nested prediction pipeline.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report instability in fitting the joint law with many parameters and underestimation from the nested step and model-size laws.

fits_no_version.finding: The ranking of data mixtures by loss shifts with model size and training steps. The longest common ordering of 20 mixtures has length only 10–11 (App. C, Fig. 11).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal pretraining data mixture is not invariant across model scale and training length.

fits_no_version.finding: Domain validation loss is an exponential function of the mixture proportions (data mixing law), with low MAE (Table 1, Figs 3, 6, 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Loss is predictable from data-mixture proportions via an exponential-linear law.

record.problems: The paper reports that nested laws can accumulate errors and that its Figure 22 predictions underestimate actual losses. Some larger-scale extrapolations are shown only in figures, without numerical error values. The joint-fit instability is described without numerical details.
record.rows_left_out: None. Data-mixing-law results, mixture optimization comparisons, and cited results from other studies were excluded because they do not directly measure the scaling-law claim.

untested.parts: Compute scaling. Data scaling beyond step counts under a fixed batch size. Most fits span under one order of magnitude; only Fig. 18 spans about four.
Extrapolation beyond about 72x in size or 6.25x in steps. Combined compute extrapolation (450x is only conjectured).
Not tested. The continual-pretraining result concerns the mixing law, not power-law scaling.
Comparison of exponents or compute-optimal splits across setups or fitting methods.

missing.what: The fitted model-size law on converged loss, L=(4.183e14/N)^0.073, has exponent 0.073 with irreducible term E=0. This is directly comparable to Kaplan's αN of about 0.076.
Fitting method: Huber loss with LBFGS over an initialisation grid, following Hoffmann et al. This is relevant for comparing fits across studies.

record.verdict_notes: Treat this as weak evidence on the scaling-law claim. The scaling-law checks are preliminary verifications of a tool, mostly over narrow ranges, with figure-only values for the largest extrapolations. The 7.25B 'converged' target was itself estimated with L(S). V7 is given no label because R7 is a qualitative remark about fitting instability.

versions.untested_parts: Compute scaling is not separately tested; the reported sweeps concern training steps and model size.
The study tests selected step and model-size extrapolations, not prediction across all models or setups.
The continual-pretraining experiment tests the study's data-mixing law, not whether power-law scaling holds in that regime or other modalities.
The paper reports instability when fitting a joint law and underestimation in its nested pipeline, but does not compare fitted exponents across setups or test compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: 70M model

conditions.value: five domains and the overall validation mixture

rows.measure: Mean absolute error of validation-loss predictions
rows.note: The paper reports this as a low mean absolute error across the validation sets; it does not give per-domain errors in the text.
rows.check: The extrapolation is only 3.3x (30k to 100k steps) on 70M models, well under the 'orders of magnitude' in V1 and V2. The MAE of 0.02 is aggregated over mixtures and domains.

rows.check: The extrapolation is tiny: fitted on 70M–305M, predicting 410M (about 1.3x). This says little about the multi-order range in V1 and V2. The Fig. 13 caption miswrites 406M.

rows.measure: Stability of fitting the scaling-law form
rows.baseline: Sequential fitting is described as empirically stable
rows.value: The joint fit was found practically unstable to fit with many parameters simultaneously.

relationships.condition: Pythia-architecture models on Pile/RedPajama mixtures; step and model-size power laws
relationships.reason: The power-law form fits and extrapolates with low error: MAE 0.02 (R1), MAE 0.003 (R2), and fits described as accurate up to 7.25B (R3–R5). Most ranges are narrow; only R5 spans orders of magnitude.
relationships.display_finding: Power-law fits and extrapolations achieved MAE of 0.02 and 0.003, with accurate predictions reported up to 7.25B parameters despite mostly narrow ranges.
